scenes.name: Nueva Orleans y los Meters
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La música de Nueva Orleans se construye de abajo arriba: batería, bajo, guitarra, vientos; la única región donde los esclavos pudieron tocar tambores desde el principio (Congo Square), de la second line al dixieland, el ragtime, el R&B y el funk. Earl Palmer, batería de Little Richard, es quizá el primer batería funk. Los Meters (Leo Nocentelli, Art Neville, George Porter Jr. y Zigaboo Modeliste) redefinieron la sencillez del riff funk con huecos de anticipación («no es lo que dices sino lo que no dices»): acompañaron a Lee Dorsey, Aaron Neville, Dr. John («Right Place, Wrong Time») y Patti LaBelle («Lady Marmalade»), y grabaron «Cissy Strut», «Look-Ka Py Py» o los discos Cabbage Alley, Rejuvenation y Fire on the Bayou, hasta un intento fallido de disco. Chocolate Milk continuó la tradición; los Neville Brothers la llevaron al gran público en los ochenta.
scenes.family: Soul y proto-funk: Stax, Nueva Orleans, Motown

podcast.title: Earl Palmer - Legendary Precision Timekeeping
podcast.body: A studio legend recounts Earl Palmer's incredible ability to precisely adjust song tempos; after a producer requested a take be two seconds shorter than 3:20, Palmer would reportedly "wind up his leg like a clock," count the new tempo, and deliver the next take exactly at 3:18. "Palmer would then pretend to wind up his leg like a clock. Count out the new tempo. And the next take would come in at three minutes eighteen, dead on."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Earl Palmer - Originator of "Funky" Term
podcast.body: Earl Palmer is reputed to be the first individual to use the term "Funky" to describe music, a testament to his distinct and influential playing style. "Earl Palmer has been claimed as the first person to use the word Funky to describe music, and he was certainly a Funky player."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Earl Palmer - Precise Timekeeper
podcast.body: Earl Palmer was recognized for his exceptionally precise timekeeping abilities as a drummer. "He was also an extraordinarily precise timekeeper."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Earl Palmer - Premier Drummer of His Era
podcast.body: Earl Palmer was widely considered the preeminent drummer in America during his active period, known for his exceptional skill and contribution to session work. "Earl Palmer, who was bar-non, the greatest drummer working in America at that time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Metronomic Time Sense
podcast.body: Drummer Earl Palmer possessed an "absolutely metronomic time sense," a skill that was crucial during the recording of Fats Domino's "Blueberry Hill." His precise timing allowed engineer Bunny Robin to seamlessly edit together a coherent version of the song from multiple half-finished takes. "thanks to the absolutely metronomic time sense of Earl Palmer, he managed to do it so well that after more than 30 years of listening to the record, I am still not certain exactly where the join is."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Transition to LA Session Work
podcast.body: Earl Palmer, a veteran drummer who had played with Little Richard, Lloyd Price, and Fats Domino in Cosimo Matassa's New Orleans studio, moved to Los Angeles and began establishing himself as a prominent session player there, including on Sam Cooke's "You Send Me" session. "Earl Palmer, who had just moved to LA from New Orleans, and was starting to make a name for himself as a session player there, after his years of playing with Little Richard, Lloyd Price, and Fats Domino in Casamon-Mutasa's studio"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
